query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the intended high-temperature operating regime? Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation, state the regime in which those predictions should hold, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Increasing the twin boundary density in FeNiCrCoCu high‐entropy alloy coatings promotes the formation of a thin, continuous oxide glaze during high‐temperature sliding, which in turn both diffuses local stress concentrations and suppresses localized plastic deformation, thereby reducing overall wear.
generation.material_initial_state: A FeNiCrCoCu coating fabricated via conventional processing that yields a baseline (standard) twin density on a conventional metal substrate (e.g., Ni).
generation.intervention: Introduce a post‐deposition thermal–mechanical treatment (for example, a rapid anneal followed by quenching) designed to enhance the density of twins within the coating.
generation.conditions: Sliding wear tests conducted in an elevated temperature regime (around 600°C) under a controlled normal load and sliding speed that mimic the intended operating conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: An increased density of twin boundaries that serve as preferential channels for oxygen diffusion and as barriers to dislocation motion.
generation.mechanism: Under high-temperature sliding, the twin boundaries accelerate local oxygen diffusion leading to the rapid formation of an adherent, protective oxide glaze layer. Concurrently, these twin boundaries distribute and alleviate localized stress, reducing plastic deformation. Thus, the cooperative mechanism of oxidation along twins and stress dispersion results in superior wear resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline coating, the twin-enhanced FeNiCrCoCu coating will show a reduction in wear loss and microscopic plastic deformation during high-temperature sliding, characterized by a smoother wear track with a uniform oxide layer and lower friction coefficient.
generation.baseline: FeNiCrCoCu coatings processed without the twin-enhancing treatment, exhibiting standard twin density.
generation.boundary: This mechanistic effect is expected to hold under high-temperature sliding conditions (near 600°C) with similar loads and speeds; outcomes under room temperature or drastically different environmental conditions may deviate due to reduced oxidation kinetics or alternative deformation modes.
generation.uncertainty: This hypothesis integrates the observed twin-induced strengthening and reduced tension–compression asymmetry in FeNiCrCoCu systems at moderate temperatures (PMC10058552::web::025::4_conclusions) with evidence of protective oxide glaze formation in high-temperature tested complex alloys (PMC10241162::web::014::remarkable_wear_resistance_and_wear_mech). Extending the role of twin boundaries to act as catalysts for rapid, protective oxidation under sliding conditions in FeNiCrCoCu coatings is novel and untested; uncertainties remain regarding the balance of diffusion kinetics and twin formation in this specific alloy matrix.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu coatings on identical substrates: one set using the standard process (baseline twin density) and the other subjected to a twin-enhancing thermal–mechanical treatment. Subject both sets to well-controlled sliding wear tests at approximately 600°C with identical loads and sliding speeds. Characterize wear loss, friction coefficients, and analyze the wear tracks for oxide glaze continuity and microstructural deformation (using SEM, TEM, XPS, and EDS).
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the twin-enhanced coatings do not demonstrate a statistically significant improvement (i.e., lower wear loss and reduced plastic deformation) and do not exhibit a more continuous and adherent oxide glaze layer compared to the baseline coatings under high-temperature conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In addition, the tensile and compression property of polycrystalline HEA with larger particle sizes is not as good as HEA with smaller particle sizes. This is attributed to the obstruction of grain boundaries and the degree of dislocation entanglement when dislocations cross grain boundaries in polycrystalline HEAs. In addition, due to the presence of grain boundaries, the stress of polycrystalline HEAs does not decrease rapidly after reaching tensile and compression limits. Finally, at 300 K, tensile and compressive loads are applied to pure nickel and nickel coated with FeNiCrCoCu HEAs. The results show that the microscopic mechanism of HEAs strengthening nickel is that the climb of dislocations in HEAs promotes the formation of twins in nickel, thereby improving the strength of nickel. After HEAs coating strengthening, the tensile-compression asymmetry of nickel was reduced by 18%. This is due to twin degradation due to the different atomic sizes of the main elements of HEA.

cited_evidence.text: No micro-pits or debris are observed from the Ni3X surface away from the worn track (Fig. S9), confirming that they are indeed generated during sliding. For NiX, its worn track dimensions also increase at 400 °C compared to those at RT, but the worn surface remains relatively smooth and is free of debris and micro-pits (Fig. S7b). This uncovers that NiX still outperforms Ni3X in resisting the elastic–plastic deformation involved with abrasive wear even at 400 °C. The higher high-temperature hardness of NiX may be responsible for the low wear rate compared to Ni3X at 400 °C (Fig. 3A). Nanoindentation tests (Fig. S2) also show that H on the worn surface of NiX (5.9 GPa) at 400 °C is higher than that of Ni3X (4.9 GPa).
